summary:
Around you are cliffs, gullies and ridges, and an astronaut cannot tell where it is safe to walk or which path is least exhausting. That is why we built a walking-route navigator for Mars.
It is based on a NASA HiRISE terrain model (~1 m resolution) and an orthoimage of a 2×2 km area, shown as a 2D map and a 3D model with slopes over 25° marked as hazards. Mars Trek (JPL) and USGS data add a geology layer and nearby science targets: gullies, RSL and hydrated minerals.
Dijkstra’s algorithm finds the route on a 250,000-point graph. Each step costs human energy from the Pandolf and Minetti equations, corrected for Martian gravity (0.38 g) and the mass of the astronaut and suit. A radiation model calibrated on Curiosity data accounts for altitude and sky blocked by slopes; the most exposed zones are avoided.
The tool compares the direct and optimal routes by calories, time, climb, cliffs and dose. On one route the direct path crosses 83 cliffs and a radiation zone, while the optimal one has no cliffs and uses 8% less energy. Everything runs in Python in the browser, with no server.
Unlike global Mars maps, our tool combines terrain, radiation and human physiology to plan real excursions, saving energy and oxygen and helping crews safely reach scientific targets, with all target locations clearly highlighted on the map.
details:
Our navigator plans walking routes for astronauts on real Martian terrain. The user sets a start and finish on a 2D map, and the tool finds the route that costs the least energy while avoiding cliffs steeper than 25° and elevated-radiation zones. It reports calories, time, climb, cliffs and radiation dose, and shows the path on a rotatable 3D model.

Benefits: instead of just a line on a map, an astronaut gets a quantified budget for each excursion. On one test route the direct path crosses 83 cliffs, while ours has none and uses 8% less energy.

Impact: our goal is to show that surface excursions can be planned around human physiology and safety, not just distance. The method works for any HiRISE terrain model, so it can help with landing-site studies, EVA planning and education.

Tools: NASA HiRISE terrain data (PDS), Mars Trek (JPL) and USGS geology. Python with numpy and scipy runs the physics and Dijkstra’s algorithm; JavaScript, Canvas and three.js handle the 2D and 3D views. Pyodide runs Python directly in the browser, so no server is needed.

Creativity: we combined three fields in one tool: terrain from orbit, the biomechanics of walking under 0.38 g, and a radiation model calibrated against Curiosity data that accounts for sky blocked by slopes.

Factors: astronaut and suit mass, Martian gravity, safe slope limits, radiation exposure, honest energy reporting without penalties, and speed fast enough to run in a browser.
